https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Labour fury at security lapses over Keir Starmer glitter protester
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.subtitle: Read our photographer’s verdict at the end
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
Labour is urgently reviewing security arrangements after a protester was able to storm the party’s conference stage and pour glitter over Sir Keir Starmer.
Yaz Ashmawi, 28, a physicist turned Extinction Rebellion strategist, was arrested after he threw glitter over Starmer as he prepared to give his keynote speech.
• The key points and policies from Starmer’s speech and Labour conference
Ashmawi, who was representing the group People Demand Democracy and was wearing a T-shirt bearing its name, ran from the back of the hall to Starmer’s podium.
The Labour leader pushed Ashmawi — whose full name is Yasine El-Ashmawi — away from the microphone as the protester grabbed Starmer’s shoulder and wrist.
It took more than ten seconds for security staff to reach the pair. When they did, he was dropped to the floor and dragged away shouting, as Rachel Reeves, the shadow chancellor, angrily said: “For god’s sake.”
Starmer has described the protester as an “idiot” and said he was “absolutely determined” to ignore him.
He told Times Radio on Wednesday: “I was absolutely determined that this wasn’t going to disrupt what has been four years of really hard work, getting the Labour Party from where we landed in 2019, which is a very bad place to this last conference before the general election, where we had to set out and did set out our positive case.”
He said he viewed the speech as a “culminating” moment. “I’ve always seen this as three stages. I took over three and a half years ago, picked it up off the floor. We had to change the party, expose the Tories and SNP as not fit to govern, then setting out the positive case, making the case that this doesn’t have to be another decade of decline.”
Starmer added: “I was determined we would get on with it. I just wanted to get on with the speech, and that’s why I rolled up my sleeves and got on with it. I didn’t want that idiot to interrupt that.”
Angela Rayner, the party’s deputy leader, said on Tuesday that she had “never seen Rachel Reeves so angry” and told LBC: “I thought I was going to do a full John Prescott at one point.”
Prescott, as deputy prime minister in 2001, punched a protester who egged him during a pro-hunting rally in Rhyl.
A Labour source said that they were “really f***ing angry” over the slow response, adding: “If he had a weapon, Keir could’ve been killed.”
A senior party source blamed the Metropolitan Police, since Starmer has round-the-clock protection. The Times understands that Met officers were in the hall during his speech as well as security staff provided by the venue, ACC Liverpool.
The Met said that it did not comment on security matters. ACC Liverpool said that “highly trained stewarding and security teams ensured the incident was dealt with appropriately”.
People Demand Democracy has been linked to Just Stop Oil and is calling for a proportional voting system for elections and a “House of Citizens” to replace the House of Lords, selected by “democratic lottery”. A Just Stop Oil insider described the group, which was set up this year, as a “coalition member”.
A representative for People Demand Democracy, who gave her name as Aria, told Times Radio: “We’re rooted in non-violence so the action was designed not to cause harm.”
However, another Labour source said: “Security didn’t work today, for whatever reason, and that’s what we’ll be reviewing with urgency.”
Graham Wettone, a former Metropolitan Police officer, said: “Anyone who gets that close is clearly a breach in security. The risk and danger depends on a number of things. Clearly, there has been a breach of security.
“But you can’t have security standing right alongside Starmer and his protection officers acted quite quickly. It comes down to how closely you want your security. It depends on what your principal wants from you, balanced with an assessment of the threat.
“The action from the cops looks fairly reasonable to me and they dealt with him quickly and reasonably. But it’s a breach of the venue’s security and questions must be asked about how the protester was able to get onto the stage.”
Those attending the conference have to have a conference pass, issued after an accreditation process, and any bags have to be scanned or searched. The security arrangements are relatively light compared with the airport-style scanners in place at the Conservative Party conference in Manchester.
A Labour spokesman said that Starmer was “fine” and “completely unfazed”. While cameras broadcasting the speech were cut as the incident unfolded, Starmer remained on stage while the man was removed. Carol Linforth, a veteran Labour staff member and the party’s director of events, helped Starmer to remove his jacket.
Starmer told members, who got to their feet to cheer and applaud: “If he thinks that bothers me, he doesn’t know me. Protest or power, that’s why we’ve changed our party, conference.”
After the speech Yvette Cooper, the shadow home secretary, said that Labour was a “party of power, not protest”. She told BBC News: “It just shows, doesn’t it, that you can’t bother Keir Starmer with stuff like that. It’s about power not protest, that is what Keir Starmer was talking about. We’re a party of power not protest.”
Last month, People Demand Democracy gave Starmer and Rishi Sunak an ultimatum to implement its demands by September 30 or face “proportionate action”.
Ashmawi, who goes by the alias “Dove”, is from Surrey and holds two master’s degrees in theoretical physics, one from the University of St Andrews and the other from the University of Cambridge.
He attended primary school in Oxted, Surrey, before moving to Dubai and studying at Dubai College, one of the Middle East’s leading private schools which charges more than £24,000 a year.
After working as a web designer, videographer and photographer, he joined Extinction Rebellion full-time as a member of the group’s strategy team.
He has previously been at the forefront of XR’s protests and in one case led protesters in a march along the River Clyde in Glasgow during Cop 26. This year he told Yahoo News UK that XR had changed and that it was “not just blocking random junctions any more” and instead “coming to the centre of power”.
The ACC Liverpool group, which runs the venue where Labour is holding its annual conference, said it “recognises the rights of all groups and individuals to free speech and freedom of expression” but said the safety of its speakers and customers was of the “utmost importance”.
Shabana Mahmood, the shadow justice minister, told BBC Radio 4’s PM programme: “I’m sure questions are being asked. We will want to make sure that nothing like that can ever happen again.”
A spokesman for Merseyside police said that Ashmawi had been arrested on suspicion of a section 39 assault, breach of the peace and causing public nuisance, and would be questioned.
At 1.20pm, everything was going to plan for Labour’s PR machine (James Glossop, Times photographer, writes). A crowd of jolly placard-wielding activists was assembled to cheer as Sir Keir Starmer and his wife Victoria walked towards a dozen or so photographers and a TV crew. This was the early picture, provided to use before the speech begins to satisfy any publications with early deadlines. It also takes place in somewhere with a bit of natural light, not something that is in abundance at party conferences.
Forty-five minutes later, things were no longer going to plan. A protester strode on to the stage in Liverpool before Starmer had even started his speech, and threw glitter all over him. This is the kind of thing we photographers need to be ready for. Although the protester’s message wasn’t particularly clear and the subsequent reporting of the speech mentioned the incident only as a side-note, I would bet that it will be the main image from the speech used in most newspapers on Wednesday morning.
Shooting a political speech is all about reading the mood of the room, weighing up where the good backgrounds are and paying attention. The most important moments to pay attention are during the first five minutes and the last five minutes. This is when ordinarily wooden politicians may start getting animated and waving to no one in particular, hugging their colleagues, gesturing to the crowd, that kind of thing. Which all make better pictures than a talking head. Had the protest happened in the middle of the speech, it may have been missed by quite a few photographers.
I decided to shoot from the back of the room, on a TV platform I probably wasn’t supposed to be on, using my 100-400mm lens at 400mm. The platform allows enough height to get clear of the audience when they stand to applaud at the beginning. It’s normally sensible to keep “on” the speaker until the cadence of their speech shifts into a more regular rhythm, and they start moving through each of the many topics they feel obliged to cover.
After this had happened there really was no point in shooting any of the standard “man points while looking serious” type pictures, so I rushed back to the laptop to file the glitter images before the paper’s important afternoon meeting, also called “conference”. One of the set held the front of our website for several hours.
I was wondering after the event if the police or party security would be in trouble for not reacting quickly enough. Starmer’s reaction in the sequence of images shows what I read to be a certain amount of disbelief at what was happening, or at least that it took seemingly so long for someone to intervene. Labour are odds on by quite a margin to win the next election. Whether they win or not, my guess is that security will be quite a bit tighter at next year’s conference.

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.title: Police drop Chris Packham goshawk chick sniff complaint
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.text:
Police have dropped an investigation into allegations that Chris Packham broke the law when he sniffed goshawk chicks on the BBC.
The naturalist was accused of potentially breaching the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 by interfering with a protected species.
Packham, 62, had been celebrating the return of goshawks, a bird of prey, to breed. He was filmed with three chicks on The One Show. After the BBC1 programme was broadcast in summer, Hampshire police received a complaint from an amateur shooting enthusiast, who questioned whether the producers were licensed to disturb rare species.
The man, who did not wish to be identified, said licences were in place for the welfare of birds “for a very good reason”. Packham was potentially disturbing the birds, he added.
The presenter had told viewers he was smelling the chick to experience its “characteristic scent”.
BBC executives were understood to believe that Packham was helping to ring, measure and weigh the chicks under trained supervision. The corporation’s position was that it did not interrupt or delay the professionals’ work.
A spokesman for Hampshire police said at the weekend that officers had seen the film “and no criminal offence was identified”. The spokesman added that the investigation had been filed.
The goshawk used to be common in England and features in the writings of Chaucer and Shakespeare. Packham lives in the New Forest, where a conservation programme has increased the number of pairs from one in 2002 to 45.
Goshawks may be removed from their nests for scientific and conservation purposes. The ringer on the BBC programme was operating under a permit from the British Trust for Ornithology.
Packham, who presents Springwatch, Autumnwatch and Winterwatch on the BBC, has become a polarising figure with his support for the environmental groups Just Stop Oil and Extinction Rebellion. He is also an outspoken opponent of hunting and has criticised grouse shooting.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Jeremy Clarkson: What do we want? A big protest! When do we want it? All the time!
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
It was a big week for the placard industry, because all over the country people were on the streets, chanting and doing protests. Some were supporting Israel. Some were supporting Palestine. And others were demanding free loft insulation for the over-50s.
There was a time when protesters used to sort of take it in turn to make their feelings known. So if you were herding some oxen up Threadneedle Street in the 14th century and you encountered an angry mob of yokels coming the other way, you’d know straight away you’d bumped into Wat Scargill’s revolting peasants who wanted an end to the class system.
And similarly, in 1913, when Emily Davison hurled herself under the King’s horse at the Epsom Derby, no one in the crowd wondered if she was protesting about Australia’s decision to put a kangaroo on its first official stamp. They knew straight away she was a suffragette because, at the time, women’s liberation was the only protest in town.
Even in my living memory, this one-at-a-time mentality was very much the way. For example, in the early 1980s, if you were driving through Berkshire and you stumbled over a bunch of hippie women with hairy armpits and a love of kumbaya folk music, you could be pretty sure they were complaining about the nuclear weapons being stored at Greenham Common.
And then later, if you found a smelly man in a tree, you’d know immediately you’d arrived at a protest about the Newbury bypass. Then, in 1990, if you found a young man with a perm making Jamie Carragher noises as he threw a chair through a shop window, you’d know straight away he was cross about Mrs Thatcher’s poll tax. It was easy back then, but now, when you run into a placard-waving mob, half the time you’ve absolutely no idea what their beef is. Until they appear the following morning on GB News to be shouted at by whatever presenter hasn’t been sacked that week.
It’s reached the point where people from Just Stop Oil can’t get to the Royal Academy to throw soup at a painting because the Tube train they intended to use has people from Extinction Rebellion sitting on top of it. And they can’t borrow their mum’s Volvo either because the roads are blocked by people who are angry about cows.
It’s ridiculous. Secondary school pupils have marched to protest against new rules on how often they can use the lavatory. We’ve had people going berserk outside the Indian high commission to protest about something that may or may not have happened in Canada. And we’ve had people who want to turn back time and rejoin the EU. And that’s before we get to the never-ending stream of people marching to support gay rights and black lives and anti-Nazism.
When there was only one thing worth protesting about at any given time, it could usually get quite a crowd. But what do the weird-beard lefties do now when they decide to spend a day mooching down Oxford Street, in the rain, with a sign? Because every day there’s a smorgasbord of options: “Hey, Humphreyetta, shall we protest about loft insulation or bankers’ bonuses today?” Surely it will get to the point where there simply aren’t enough socialists to go round.
And to make everything even more complicated, every day someone invents a new “issue” on social media or starts a new “conversation” about something that’s been considered normal for four million years. And that’s it. On with the high-visibility jacket. Out with the Day-Glo marker pen. And off we go to shout at a policeman woman and throw a plant pot through a window at HSBC.
All of which brings me on to that Herbert who stormed the stage at the Labour Party conference in Liverpool last week and threw glitter into Sir Starmer’s Playmobil hair. Let’s look first of all at what must have gone through his head. As a committed and enthusiastic protester, he’d woken up and assessed the situation. Hamas had attacked Israel and committed a number of atrocities. Israel had responded with a bombardment that beggared belief. But he decided this wasn’t worth the effort.
Nor was the continuing war in Ukraine or the recent decision to get more oil from the North Sea or Katie Hopkins’s view that women don’t have an inalienable right to have penises. He wasn’t even going to throw in his oar with those who want more Blue Peter dinghies to land on the beaches of Kent. No. He decided he’d make a protest about how there are no “people” in government. “We demand a people’s house,” he yelled. Not sure who the “we” was, but we’ll let that drop.
What are “we” suggesting? That “people” stand as candidates and then other “people” vote for them? Or by “people” does he mean “people” like him? If he does, he’s got a problem. Because it’s hard to serve in a “people’s house” when you are glued to a roundabout in Fulham. Maybe, then, he means “people” like me. Though somehow I doubt that.
I’m sure, however, all will become clear when he appears on what’s left of GB News to explain himself. I’m also sure his protest will wither and die like pretty well every other protest that’s ever been staged. Remember the Countryside Alliance march through London? About 400,000 went on that, to complain about a proposed ban on hunting, and what happened? Hunting was banned.
Then you had the anti-Iraq war march. That was even bigger. Some say a million turned up — and did it work? Well, we went to war with Iraq, so no. Not really. And if a million people can’t change the government’s mind, what chance does a lone Herbert in Liverpool have? And what chance do the loft insulation people have, or the Just Stop Oilers? You can think about that next time you drive down the Newbury bypass, knowing that we still have a class system, protected by a bunch of submarines armed with nuclear weapons.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/gret.title: Greta Thunberg arrested at London protest against oil bosses
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/gret.text:
Greta Thunberg has been arrested by police after leading protests outside a central London hotel that was hosting the heads of the world’s largest oil and gas companies.
The environmental activist was among 29 people arrested at a protest outside the InterContinental London hotel on Park Lane, which was hosting the annual Energy Intelligence Forum, an oil industry conference.
Thunberg, 20, was led away from the hotel by Metropolitan Police officers and placed in the back of a marked van. Activists shouted “thank you Greta” as she was searched.
Speakers at the annual event, which until 2019 was known as Oil & Money, included the chief executive of Saudi state oil giant Aramco, Amin Nasser, and senior executives from BP.
Shell’s chief executive, Wael Sawan, had been due to attend the conference early in the afternoon but instead appeared by video link in light of the protests.
Protesters said that Thunberg was arrested while linking arms and chanting with others outside the entrance and said that she had been taken to Wandsworth police station.
Those arrested were detained for offences including obstruction of the highway, criminal damage, breaches under section 14 of the Public Order Act and breach of court bail conditions.
The demonstration was organised by Fossil Free London and involved dozens of protesters blocking access to the hotel, with protesters holding banners, shouting “oily money out” and “cancel the conference”, while others lit yellow and pink smoke flares.
Activists from Greenpeace abseiled from the roof of the hotel to unfurl a banner reading “make big oil pay”.
A white fence surrounded the hotel entrance and kept protesters out while police attempted to escort conference attendees through the crowd of chanting activists.
The protesters claim that fossil fuel companies are deliberately slowing the global energy transition to renewables in order to make more profit.
Nuri Syed Corser, of Fossil Free London, said: “We need direct action to take back the power from the oil elite that has gathered here today behind closed doors. Their only plan is to profit at our expense. Arrests like these will not deter us. Our right to protest is our own, it is not given to us by the government.”
Addressing reporters before her arrest, Thunberg said: “The world is drowning in fossil fuels. Our hopes and dreams and lives are being washed away by a flood of greenwashing and lies.
“It has been clear for decades that the fossil fuel industries were well aware of the consequences of their business models, and yet, they have done nothing.
“The opposite – they have actively delayed, distracted and denied the causes of the climate crisis and spread doubts about their own engagement in it.”
Thunberg added: “We cannot let this continue. The elite of the oil and money conference, they have no intention of transition.
“Their plan is to continue this destructive search of profits. That is why we have to take direct action to stop this and to kick oil money out of politics.
“We have no other option but to put our bodies outside this conference and to physically disrupt. And we have to do that every time, we have to continue showing them that they are not going to get away with this.”
Maja Darlington, a campaigner at Greenpeace UK, said: “Big oil is profiting from humanity’s loss and those who have done the least to cause climate change are being forced to pay the price.”
The Met said officers had “continued discussions with the protesters” and made “interventions” to enable members of the public safe access in and out of the venue.
“Officers on scene have kept this under constant review and at 12.32pm imposed conditions on the group under section 14 of the Public Order Act given to prevent serious disruption to the community, hotel and guests,” he said.
“Officers asked the protesters to move from the road onto the pavement, which would enable them to continue with their demonstration without breaching the conditions. A number of protesters failed to do so and we have now made a further 14 arrests for section 14 of the Public Order Act and a further one for criminal damage. Officers remain on scene.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/gret.title: Greta Thunberg charged over oil protest in London
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/gret.subtitle: Campaigner set for court appearance next month
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/gret.text:
Greta Thunberg has been charged with a public order offence after leading a protest outside a central London hotel hosting heads of the world’s largest oil and gas companies.
The environmental activist is one of 26 people who were charged over a protest outside the InterContinental London hotel on Park Lane, which was hosting the annual Energy Intelligence Forum, an oil industry conference.
The alleged offences involved in the protest include obstructing the highway and failing to comply with a condition imposed under Section 14 of the Public Order Act.
Thunberg, 20, was led away from the hotel by Metropolitan Police officers, who arrested 29 people in total, and placed in the back of a marked van.
Protesters shouted “thank you Greta” as the activist was being searched.
The Metropolitan Police said Thunberg, whose address was given as Dorset, was charged with failing to comply with a condition imposed under Section 14 of the Public Order Act. She and other activists were bailed to appear at Westminster magistrates’ court on November 15.
The demonstration was organised by Fossil Fuel London and involved dozens of protesters blocking access to the hotel, with protesters holding banners, shouting “oily money out” and “cancel the conference”, while others lit yellow and pink smoke flares.
Activists from Greenpeace abseiled down from the roof of the hotel to unfurl a banner reading “Make big oil pay” during the demonstration.
The protesters claim that fossil fuel companies are deliberately slowing the global energy transition to renewables to make more profit.
A white fence surrounded the hotel entrance and kept protesters out of the hotel while police attempted to escort conference attendees through the crowd of chanting activists.
Fossil Fuel London said that Thunberg was among six protesters who were released from Wandsworth police station at 2am. The group said that some protesters were given bail conditions preventing them from entering Westminster until their court appearance in November.
Speakers at the annual event, which until 2019 was known as Oil & Money, included the chief executive of Saudi state oil giant Aramco and senior executives from BP.
Shell’s chief executive Wael Sawan had been due to attend the conference but instead appeared by videolink in light of the protests.
A spokeswoman for the Met said: “Officers responded to the protest on the morning of Tuesday, 17 October and imposed conditions to prevent disruption to the public. The protesters were asked to move from the road on to the pavement, which would enable them to continue with their demonstration without breaching the conditions. One woman, who was arrested on suspicion of criminal damage, has been bailed pending further enquiries”.
Usually, charges for failing to comply with section 14 of the Public Order Act are dealt with through a fine, although the maximum sentence is six months’ imprisonment.
Last week, a Swedish court found Thunberg guilty of disobeying a police order to leave a climate protest and fined her £335.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Labour party conference: Starmer pledges to ‘break the stranglehold of Tory decline’ — as it happened
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
Keir Starmer has vowed to “break the stranglehold of Tory decline” and issued a direct appeal to moderate Conservative voters to back Labour at the next election.
The Labour leader said that he wanted the nation to “walk towards a decade of national renewal” and “face down the age of insecurity”.
He appealed to Tory voters who “look in horror” as their party descends into the “murky waters of populism and conspiracy” to turn to Labour as the natural party of government.
He said: “If you feel our country needs a party that conserves, that fights for our union, our environment, the rule of law, family life… let me tell you, Britain already has one, and you can join it. It’s this Labour Party.”
Pitching himself as the heir to new Labour, Starmer contrasted “13 years of things can only get better” with “13 years of “things have only got worse”.
He said: “Why Labour? Because we serve your interests. Why Labour? Because we will grow every corner of our country. Why Labour? Because we have a plan to take back our streets, switch on Great British Energy, get the NHS back on its feet, tear down the barriers to opportunity and get Britain building again.
“A plan for a Britain built to last, a plan to heal the wounds, a plan to turn the page and say in a cry of defiance to all those who now write out country off. Britain must, Britain can, Britain will get its future back.”
Starmer’s speech was briefly disrupted before it had begun by a protester who took to the stage and threw green glitter over him.
Lord Mandelson, one of the key architects of New Labour, has said that next year’s general election is Labour’s to lose (Seren Hughes writes).
When asked in the aftermath of Sir Keir Starmer’s conference speech whether that was the case, the Labour peer told Times Radio: “I think that’s a reasonable way of putting it.”
The former cabinet minister said he believes the Conservatives will lose their majority and had not met a single Tory in the past six months “who doesn’t share that view”. But he admitted that Labour has work to do to secure a majority.
“They’ve basically given up,” he said of the Tories. “They’re throwing in the towel and they’re busy fighting amongst themselves over who will succeed Rishi Sunak after the next election. But that doesn’t mean to say that Labour has yet built up and created its own majority in parliament in order to govern as it wishes.
“That work has still to be done. It’s going to be done over the coming year. But what you heard today was the sort of passion and conviction and content and hard-nosed policy work that Keir Starmer is going to continue to lay before the British people.”
“Optimism, one sensed, does not come naturally to him, but he did his best. He sounded like a man who, if he didn’t quite yet have a fully developed plan to vanquish them, has at least understood the country’s problems,” according to Juliet Samuel.
Philip Collins, meanwhile, argued: “It was, however, a speech that stuttered just as it started. Grand arguments were flirted with but left undeveloped. There was a recurring, gently populist, theme of the people v the government.”
And Iain Martin observed: “Starmer displayed a level of confidence and dexterity that just a few months ago seemed beyond him. This was a well-structured address making a coherent, patriotic, serious argument about the challenges Labour will face if it becomes the government after next year’s election.”
A protester has been arrested on suspicion of assault, breaching the peace and causing a public nuisance after he disrupted Sir Keir Starmer’s conference speech (Ali Mitib writes).
Yaz Ashmawi, 28, a physicist turned Extinction Rebellion activist from Surrey, stormed the stage wearing a T-shirt featuring the logo of People Demand Democracy, a Just Stop Oil-style campaign group. He threw glitter over the Labour leader before being removed by security guards in what has been described as a major security failing.
The group is demanding a proportional voting system for elections and wants to create a legally binding national “House of Citizens” selected by “democratic lottery”. A Just Stop Oil insider described the group, which was set up this year, as a “coalition member”.
In a statement released through JSO channels, the group said: “A House of Citizens will realign power in society. It will empower people to set the agenda, guide policies and keep politicians in check.
“We all need a chance for a seat at the table. We all deserve a voice in the room. A People’s House brings people together like a jury and provides the time to hear from experts and scientists to decide what policy is best for everyone.”
Sir Keir Starmer ended his speech by promising to “face down an age of insecurity” and “break the stranglehold of Tory decline” (Chris Smyth and Matt Dathan write).
He promised voters that Labour will “serve your interests”, saying they should back his party because they would “grow every corner of our country”, “take back our streets, switch on Great British energy, get the NHS back on its feet, tear down the barriers to opportunity and get Britain building again”.
Starmer warned his party they must be disciplined in order to win the election because the Conservative party was prepared to “scorch the earth” just to stay in power.
He said the Tories had “completely severed its relationship with the future” but said his party would need to be prepared as the Conservative are “always up for the fight to save their own skins”.
Starmer warned: “This isn’t over. In fact, it’s barely begun. So we have to be disciplined, focused, ready to fight back and confident, conference, because we have come so far already.”
Labour can win the next election by beating the SNP in Scotland, Starmer has said (George Grylls writes).
The Labour leader said Scotland “can lead the way to a Labour government” following the party’s win in the Rutherglen & Hamilton West by-election. “For the first time in a long time, we can see a tide that is turning,” he said.
He warned that the SNP will “regroup” after the by-election defeat and said the party would “try to present nationalism as a bridge to the world”.
“We have to remind them, it can barely provide a ferry out of the Hebrides,” he said.
Starmer said that government “must steer the ship on industrial policy” as he contrasted his interventionist industrial strategy with the “stand-aside state” of the Conservatives (Chris Smyth and Steven Swinford write).
Attacking the “drift, stagnate, decline” cycle under the Conservatives, he said that laissez-faire government “leaves nobody with the future they want because there’s no direction and irresponsibility towards the future”.
He promised a three-point plan for growth, with a national wealth fund investing in green jobs, stability for investors and research and a renewed focus on skills.
And he pledged Labour would “speed ahead” with the climate mission. “Clean British energy is cheaper than foreign fossil fuels,” he said. “That means cheaper bills for every family in the country.”
He added: “So when Rishi Sunak says row back on our climate mission, I say speed ahead. Speed ahead with investments, with half a million jobs”.
Labour will push ahead with creating Great British Energy, a public owned company.
The protester who disrupted Labour leader Sir Keir Starmer’s conference speech is part of a new Just Stop Oil-style campaign group (Ali Mitib and Peter Chappell write).
The organisation, called People Demand Democracy, are demanding a proportional voting system for elections and want to create a legally-binding national “House of Citizens”, selected by “democratic lottery”.
The activist, who stormed the stage wearing a People Demand Democracy T-shirt, is called Yaz Ashmawi. He was removed from the conference by the police.
A Just Stop Oil insider described the group, that was set up this year, as a “coalition member”.
In a statement released through JSO channels, the group said: “A House of Citizens will realign power in society, it will empower people to set the agenda, guide policies and keep politicians in check.
“We all need a chance for a seat at the table, we all deserve a voice in the room.
“A People’s House brings people together like a jury, and provides the time to hear from experts and scientists to decide what policy is best for everyone.”
Sir Keir Starmer has promised a “competitive tax regime” under Labour as he celebrated the party’s close ties with business (George Grylls and Matt Dathan write).
The Labour leader said the “barriers of dogma” would not stop the party from engaging with the private sector and he said he wanted to “hold out the hand of partnership to business”.
Starmer said economic growth was an “iron law” of Labour under his leadership but he said unlike during the 1980s the benefits would be “working people everywhere”.
He added that fiscal responsibility is “non negotiable,” Keir Starmer said as he insisted a Labour government would put investment at the heart of its economic policy.
He said he has lost count of the number of conversations he has had with chief executives who have bemoaned the “chopping and changing” and short-term decisions that was holding back investment in the UK.
The Labour leader said his government would set up a national wealth fund that would work “hand in glove” with the private sector to rebuild the economy. But he insisted that the British public must “share the rewards” of business investment, so he will allow people to retain a stake in public investments.
Starmer declared Labour would “bulldoze” through the planning system as he said restrictions on building were turning home-ownership into “a luxury for the few” (Chris Smyth writes).
Promising “the next generation of Labour new towns”, he said his government would take inspiration from “old Labour ideas” that had spurred the creation of places like Stevenage and Milton Keynes after the second world war.
“There will be resistance from people who say, ‘no, we don’t want Britain’s future here’. My message to them is this, a future must be built,” Starmer insisted.
Starmer said that Britain’s failure to build was “an obstacle to the aspirations of millions now and in the future, who deserve the security of home ownership.”
Labour will not “tear up” the green belt, Sir Keir said, but will end “ridiculous uses” of it such as car parks and low-quality land.
He said “Labour is the party that protects our green spaces”, citing his own childhood in Surrey. But he said that protecting “dreary wasteland” within city boundaries “cannot be justified as a reason to hold our future back.”
Sir Keir Starmer has said government “can make or break a life” as he defended the need for state involvement in areas such as workers’ rights.
The Labour leader said inequality was “corrosive” and he said government could be “a force for good”.
“We can fight alongside working people in the name of justice and opportunity,” he said.
“I’ve looked into the eyes of the people that we must serve at the Crown Prosecution Service [and] in my work in Northern Ireland. And I’ve seen reflected back the knowledge the government can make or break a life it’s that responsibility that drives me on towards the reforms I know we must make.”
Sir Keir Starmer branded Rishi Sunak one of the “shallow men” of Westminster who are out of touch and cannot understand the lives of ordinary men and women (Matt Dathan writes).
He said he and the Conservatives “can’t change” and “couldn’t even change during a pandemic, when our country came together to follow rules, rules that they set and they broke”.
“The walls of Westminster are so high,” Starmer said. “The view that your lives, your services, your future are just pieces on their board — that’s so deeply ingrained in their mindset. They have no way to understand what you’ve been through.”
He added: “Rishi Sunak and the shallow men and women of Westminster are unable to see, unable to listen, unable to stand in your shoes and serve this country, and they won’t change.”
Sir Keir Starmer has defended Labour’s decision to charge VAT on private school fees, saying it would “shatter the glass ceiling” (George Grylls and Steven Swinford write).
The Labour leader denounced critics who have urged the party not to “rock the boat”. He said levying the tax on independent schools would allow more mental health staff and specialised teachers in state schools.
He said that after 13 years of Conservative rule public services had been “cut to the bone”. He added that reforming “wasteful procurement” in the police would allow Labour to fight antisocial behaviour with more neighbourhood patrols.
Starmer added he wanted to build a Britain where people can be “certain things will be better for your children”.
He said “At some point in your life, many people here will have heard a nagging voice inside saying: ‘No this isn’t for you. You don’t belong here. You can’t do that’.
“In some ways, it’s the hardest class ceiling of all. Conference. Imagine if instead, a whole country said you do belong. Imagine if our whole country said we back your potential”
Starmer said that the NHS has become a “sickness service” and cannot be put on a pedestal (Steven Swinford and Matt Dathan write).
“I know some people don’t like the word reform but I tell you now, there’s no other option,” he said. “We must be the government that finally transforms our NHS. We can’t go on with a sickness service.”
He said that Labour will use technology to “overhaul every aspect of delivery”, move care closer to communities and use artificial
intelligence to “spot disease quickly”.
He said Labour will consign “dangerous” waits for cancer treatment to history.
Starmer added it was an “outrage” that there are seven million people waiting for treatment as he cited a semi-professional footballer who plays for Hendon who tore his knee ligaments so badly that it left him with a choice of paying £15,000 to go private or abandoning his career.
Starmer said: “How will it come to this? Working people paying for their own health care? In a cost-of-living crisis? Pensioners waiting weeks, months, sometimes waiting years just for the care that they need?”
Sir Keir Starmer has said voters are “crying out for change” as he warned that it would take a decade to repair the country’s “crumbling public realm”.
The Labour leader said the British public “need change, want change, cry out for change”.
But he warned that government was “not like ticking a box” and said long-term solutions were not “oven ready” – a reference to Boris Johnson’s famous description of the Conservatives’ Brexit deal in the 2019 general election.
Referring back to previous occasions when Labour took power, Starmer said the party would need a decade to turn the country around.
“If you think our job in 1997 was to rebuild a crumbling public realm, but in 1964 it was to modernise an economy left behind by the pace of technology, but in 1945, to build a new Britain out of the trauma of collective sacrifice, then in 2024 it will have to be all three,” he said.
He added: “A decade of national renewal. That’s what it will take.”
The cost-of-living crisis is denying people the joys of life, the Labour leader said. He recalled his own holiday this summer in the Lake District (Steven Swinford writes).
“I was eating fish and chips,” he said. “We were sitting there, it was calm. It was beautiful.
“The Lake District never lets you down. I went there every year as a child with my family and although she struggled so much to walk, my mum loved the lakes. So it was really special to share it with my kids”.
He said that on his first day back from holiday he had spoken to a single mother in Worthing who was in “survival mode”.
“That’s what this cost of living crisis does,” he said. “It intrudes on the little things that we love, whittles away at our joy — days out, meals out, holidays.”
Starmer declared “we are the healers” as he promised to shelter Britain from the “storm” of global insecurity (Chris Smyth writes).
In what has been seen as an acknowledgement that taxes should not rise, Starmer said: “We should never forget that politics should tread lightly on people’s lives, that our job is to shoulder the burden for working people, carry the load not add to it.”
But Starmer also sought to harness people’s exhaustion with politics and global crisis, saying voters “want to know, can we find that elusive path to an economy that serves their community? Can we deliver the rock of stability they need to move forward with their lives?”
He promised that amid “all the change and insecurity” he would “find the hunger to win new opportunities, and the strength to conserve what is precious”.
Sir Keir Starmer said he was appalled by the “senseless murder” of Israeli men, women and children by Hamas “terrorists” (George Grylls writes).
The Labour leader drew applause from the audience of party members as he said the attacks by militants had done “nothing” for the Palestinian cause.
“I am shocked and appalled by the events in Israel. I utterly condemn the senseless murder of men, women and children, including British citizens in cold blood by the terrorists of Hamas,” he said.
“This party believes in the two-state solution: a Palestinian state alongside a safe and secure Israel.
“But this action by Hamas does nothing for Palestinians and Israel must always have the right to defend her people.”
Starmer said the world was becoming “a more volatile place” as he warned of a “new age of insecurity”, drawing a link with the small boats crisis in the Channel.
Starmer criticised his predecessor, Jeremy Corbyn, who he said had transformed Labour into a “party of protest” (Chris Smyth and Steven Swinford write).
He said that his Labour would take an “entirely new” approach to politics. “Conference, this new path could only be walked by a new party, a changed Labour Party, no longer in thrall to gesture politics, no longer a party of protest. A party of service.”
He said that Labour had been “rebuilt” and “renewed”. “We’ve connected to an old partnership, a bargain that we serve working people as they drive our country forward,” he said. “And that’s why we had to change so fast. Why we had to fight so hard to change this party.”
He promised a “Britain built to last, with higher growth, safer streets cheap, British power in your home, more opportunity in your community, the NHS off its knees”.
The Labour leader condemned “13 years of decline” under the Conservative party and promised a decade of “national renewal” under Labour.
He accused Rishi Sunak of offering the “the gnawing rot of despair” at the Conservative party conference last week and said the prime minister had “winnowed the confidence” of the nation.
“I believe in this country, I believe in its spirit, in its people, in its businesses,” he said.
“I don’t just see the boards going up in our high streets. I see the businesses, the pubs, the cafes, still find a way through the chaos still trading a way of serving their community.”
Sir Keir Starmer opened his conference speech with an attack on Rishi Sunak and the Conservatives.
“What can you say about a prime minister who goes to Manchester to cancel Manchester’s train line,” he asked.
“A self-declared champion of motorists who had to borrow a car for a photo op.
“A man who keeps a very close watch on the cost of living crisis from the vantage point of a short haul helicopter. Conference, I never thought I’d say this but I’m beginning to see why Liz Truss won.”
He said that while Labour had offered 13 years of “things can only get better”, the Tories had overseen 13 years of “things have only got worse”.
The queue for Sir Keir Starmer’s conference speech is currently snaking out of the main conference centre in Liverpool.
Labour members are patiently waiting for the opportunity to see their party leader deliver his keynote speech — but many are set to be disappointed owing to the demand.
The end of the queue, about 30 minutes before the speech was due to start, is outside the conference centre on the banks of the River Mersey.
Yvette Cooper warned rapists and domestic abusers “the police will be after you” under a Labour government as she shared a story of her great-great-grandmother who was attacked by her husband (Matt Dathan writes).
The shadow home secretary said she was “sick and tired” of women who faced abuse and violence “being failed” generation after generation.
She said a Labour government would put rape investigation units in every force, domestic abuse experts in every 999 call centre and would require police forces to use tactics normally reserved for terrorist investigations.
Sharing a personal story, Cooper said: “My great-great-grandmother was attacked by her husband. First when she was pregnant. The report says he struck and kicked her so she could not sit or lie in bed.
“Then he attacked her with a poker. In front of her daughter. The case went to court, the magistrates bound him over to keep the peace.
“But you know the most shocking thing about that story? That is more protection from the police and courts than many domestic abuse victims get today.”
Sir Keir Starmer has enjoyed a bewildering range of celebrity endorsements at the Labour Party conference — from Mary “Queen of Shops” Portas to Mark Carney, the former governor of the Bank of England (George Grylls writes).
But hours before Starmer’s appearance on the main stage in Liverpool, Labour has unveiled its latest trump card: Will Young, the winner of 2002’s edition of Pop Idol.
Referencing some of his more obscure hits including Evergreen Prosperity and Your Games, Young joked about his support for Labour in a video released by the party. “I don’t think Labour are interested in playing games, I think they take this very seriously,” he said.
Young also said he had “just got here, so I don’t want to leave so I’m not leaving right now” — a reference to the 2003 hit Leave Right Now.
The pop singer, 44, is at the conference campaigning for an end to animal testing.
Rishi Sunak’s migration policy is an attempt to “deflect from 13 years of abject failure”, the shadow immigration minister has said (George Grylls writes).
Stephen Kinnock said the government saw asylum seekers as a “wedge issue” and was using it “to set communities against each other — to divide, to dehumanise”.
“I think their strategy is backfiring in a very big way because the more they focus public attention on the issue, the more they expose the utter incompetence, neglect and arrogance that they have shown over the last 13 years,” Kinnock told a fringe event at the Labour conference.
It is dangerous for our economy for Britain to be “sitting on the sidelines whilst others are in the global race for the jobs and industries of the future”, Rachel Reeves has said (Geraldine Scott writes).
The shadow chancellor told a Labour conference fringe event that Britain was facing a “moron premium” following Liz Truss’s disastrous mini-Budget which meant it was now more expensive for Britain to borrow than other countries.
She said that if “anyone was in any doubt” over Labour’s economic plans, they should take comfort that Truss wrote a newspaper column criticising them.
“Thanks Liz,” Reeves said.
Labour MPs will be instructed to support Rishi Sunak’s plans to ban smoking (George Grylls writes).
Wes Streeting, the shadow health secretary, said Labour MPs would be whipped to support lifting the legal age to buy cigarettes by one year every year, so that children aged 14 and under will never be able to buy them.
Sunak has said he will give Conservative MPs a free vote, meaning they will not be obliged to support the government.
Liz Truss, the former prime minister, is among those who have already suggested they will rebel.
Streeting told a fringe event at Labour conference: “I know he’s given Liz (Truss) a free vote because the Conservative Party sadly dances to the tune of Nigel Farage these days, quite literally.
“But the good news I can offer Rishi Sunak is that when it comes to that free vote, Labour will be whipping, we’ll be whipping in favour and we will deliver the votes he needs.
“So this generation of children grow up smoke free and are in fact even less likely to smoke than they are to vote Conservative.”
The war in Israel has threatened to overshadow the Labour conference in Liverpool (George Grylls writes).
But in a measure of how far the Labour Party has transformed under Starmer’s leadership, pro-Palestinian protests have been almost entirely restricted to outside the conference venue.
Shadow cabinet ministers have repeatedly denounced Hamas militants as “terrorists” and insisted upon Israel’s right to defend itself.
Yesterday, David Lammy, the shadow foreign secretary, rushed back to London to address a vigil for Israeli victims of the attacks.
Starmer will say in his speech that he runs “a changed Labour Party, no longer in thrall to gesture politics, no longer a party of protest… Those days are done. We will never go back.”
Sir Keir Starmer has tucked into a continental breakfast with his wife Victoria as he prepares for his conference speech this afternoon (George Grylls writes).
The Labour leader released a picture of himself looking relaxed with a pot of tea and a croissant.
Starmer has ruled out an appearance by Victoria from his conference stage later today after Akshata Murty, Rishi Sunak’s wife, introduced the prime minister at Conservative conference.
In an interview with the Sunday Mirror, Starmer said he valued the privacy of his family life, joking: “I don’t think I’d put her through that.”
Talking about his wife, who works in occupational health for the NHS, Starmer said: “She’s a streetwise, grounded, brilliant, gorgeous woman who wants as far as she can to get on with her own life and to protect it,” he said.
Labour would create a legal advocate for rape victims in every police force area, the shadow justice secretary has announced (George Grylls writes).
Shabana Mahmood said rape victims were being “systematically failed” by the current system.
She said victims were facing an average wait of about two years before their cases went to trial.
“Labour’s legal advocates will ensure victims’ rights are upheld,” she said.
“This would mark the most transformative change to the status of rape victims within the justice system.”
“The introduction of legal advocates will drive down drop-out rates and help bring perpetrators to justice, increase prosecutions and make our streets safe.”
Mahmood also confirmed Labour would match the government’s commitment to build 20,000 prison places.
The Conservatives have presided over a “multiverse of crapness”, Emily Thornberry has said (George Grylls writes).
The shadow attorney general said the UK was trapped in a “never-ending loop of Tory incompetence”.
“The economy’s still wrecked. The rivers are still full of sewage. Waiting lists are still rising. Schools are still falling apart,” Thornberry said in a speech to the conference.
“It’s like we’re trapped in some never-ending time loop of Tory incompetence. The Groundhog Day of gross dereliction. The multiverse of crapness.”
Thornberry has said she would review the rights of women with no joint property or parental responsibilities who are in couples who can be evicted when their relationship ends.
“No woman should be forced to get married or stay in an unhappy relationship just to avoid ending up on the street,” she said.
Thornberry also formally announced she is being advised by Marina Wheeler, the human rights barrister and former wife of Boris Johnson, about tackling sexual harassment in the workplace.
“All of us sharing the belief that no woman should have to live in fear, no woman should have to suffer in silence, and no woman should have to hope for the best when it comes to keeping a roof over her head,” Thornberry said.
Labour is neck and neck with the SNP in Scotland, a YouGov poll has found, (George Grylls writes).
In a further boost to Sir Keir Starmer following Labour’s recent win in the Rutherglen & Hamilton West by-election, a poll has found that the gap has narrowed in Scotland to just one point.
In total, 33 per cent of voters back the SNP compared to 32 per cent for Labour, the YouGov survey for the Scottish Fabians shows.
In his speech, Starmer is expected to say Labour’s by-election win in Scotland demonstrates the party can keep the union together.
“For the first time in a long time we can see a tide that is turning,” he is expected to say.
“Four nations that are renewing. Old wounds of division - exploited by the Tories and the SNP - beginning to heal. Let the message from Rutherglen ring out across Britain: Labour serves working people in Scotland because Labour serves working people across all these islands.”
Sir Keir Starmer will set out plans for 13,000 more neighbourhood police officers in his speech today (George Grylls writes).
The Labour leader will reaffirm his commitment to get “more police in your town, fighting antisocial behaviour, taking back our streets”.
The Community Policing Guarantee will promise more patrols of town centres with a total of 13,000 more neighbourhood police and police community support officers. The announcement is one of Starmer’s five “missions” for a Labour government. The others are growth, clean energy, NHS and equality of opportunity.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/education/ar.title: Just Stop Oil allowed to recruit at Oxford University freshers’ fair
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/education/ar.text:
Oxford University’s student union has allowed Just Stop Oil to potentially recruit new members by hosting a table at its freshers’ fair.
The climate change protest group manned a small stall at the two-day event this week alongside a number of talks aimed at bolstering its membership.
Members of the group, which routinely targets public events to attract attention, have long regarded universities as key recruitment grounds.
The group is holding a series of “student welcome talks” in Oxford over coming weeks, including one with Roger Hallam, the co-founder of Extinction Rebellion and now a leader in Just Stop Oil.
This is part of a wider six-week push at universities across the country aimed at recruiting enough new members to “overwhelm” police at street protests in coming weeks.
Last month, Gillian Keegan, the education secretary, wrote to vice-chancellors encouraging them to ensure students were “aware of the consequences” of engaging in illegal protest. She said they should be aware of a “heightened risk of unlawful activity” on campuses.
The group’s small stall at the Oxford Student Union this week was manned by Daniel Knorr, a 21-year-old biochemistry student who has attracted media attention for his stunts. The activist was carried off the pitch at Lord’s by the England cricketer Jonny Bairstow in June after he and two other protestors ran on to the pitch during the second Ashes Test.
The student also posted 17,000 leaflets to students via their college cubby holes this week, the Daily Mail reported.
Knorr told the Daily Mail: “We are asking fellow students to take part in nonviolent civil resistance. Young people will live to experience the worst effects of climate breakdown.
“I hope Oxford University continues to enable freedom of thought and assembly to its students.”
The union vets students who apply to host a stall at the freshers’ event for a small fee. A spokesman for the union said: “The last two days have seen over 10,000 students attend the Oxford SU freshers’ fair.
“Oxford SU is a proud supporter of free speech and as such would never deny any student society the opportunity to have a stall at our freshers’ fair on a first come first serve basis.’
Oxford University said that it supported freedom of speech but not illegal protest. A spokesman said: “Oxford University supports the right of all our students and student groups to express views of all persuasions within the law.
“The university does not support illegal action, including any unlawful protesting, and may, within its powers, take any steps it considers appropriate against any student guilty of such behaviour.”
Leaked emails recently revealed how the climate group, which wants the government to stop issuing new fossil fuel licenses, is actively courting student members for new protest actions.
After a slump in its attention-seeking protests in recent weeks, the group is gearing up for a so-called slow march through London later this month on what it says will be an “unprecedented scale”.
The emails suggest that the group plans for 3,000 protesters to be arrested during the action, of which it would like about 500 to be students. The “strategy for student mobilisation” plan stated that this number of arrests would overwhelm police stations and the courts, forcing the government to address its demands.
It further outlined how the group would launch a “massive push” around fresher’s week through talks and potentially carrying out disruptive actions. This is to be followed, the leak stated, by a “dynamite turbo boost” of actions around campus, including spray-painting university buildings with fake oil.
Welcome talks have been lined up by the group at universities in Exeter, Birmingham, Plymouth, Lewisham, Bristol and York over the coming weeks.
Oxford students have previously taken part in Just Stop Oil stunts. The university’s earth sciences department hosted activist Phoebe Plummer, who made headlines for throwing soup at a Van Gogh painting, for a talk in May.
Oxford’s new vice-chancellor, Professor Irene Tracey, declared climate change “the greatest challenge of our time” in an oration earlier this week.
On Wednesday, five Just Stop Oil activists were arrested after they disrupted a performance of Les Misérables in the West End of London. Four young protesters were loudly booed after they invaded the stage at the Sondheim Theatre then unveiled large orange banners and shouted campaign slogans. The cast tried to continue before the music stopped and they were rushed backstage.
The activists stood shouting “Just Stop Oil”, but were quickly drowned out by angry audience members, who whistled, booed and heckled them, yelling: “Get off, you stupid people,” and “How dare you!”
As the curtain came down the protesters locked themselves to the set, prompting the theatre to be evacuated.
• Five people have been charged with aggravated trespass after Just Stop Oil protesters disrupted a performance of Les Misérables in London’s West End.
On Thursday night, the Metropolitan Police identified Hannah Taylor, 23, Lydia Gribbin, 28, Hanan Ameur, 22, Noah Crane, 18, and Poppy Bliss, 19, as the activists involved in the stunt. The group was videoed storming the Sondheim Theatre’s stage on Wednesday.
The five activists have been bailed to appear at Westminster magistrates’ court on November 3.

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/music/a.title: Who are Labour’s new MPs Sarah Edwards and Alistair Strathern?
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/music/a.text:
Sarah Edwards, the fresh-faced winner of the Tamworth by-election, received high-profile support during her election battle.
Sporting trendy glasses and a corduroy shirt, the singer Will Young recorded a video for Edwards, a trade union organiser, while visiting this month’s Labour conference, describing her as a “fresh start”.
Another wellspring of support came from Ross Kemp, inexplicably in a caravan park. The former EastEnders hardman recorded a video of support for Edwards on polling day while surrounded by static caravans.
In it, he praised her for “delivering for the people of Tamworth”. He added: “It’s going to be close but you have the opportunity to vote for a difference in your constituency today.”
Aged 35, her online CV on LinkedIn features 17 board, trustee, governor positions at organisations from the NHS to the National Farmers Union.
Edwards grew up in Moseley, a suburb of Birmingham, before attending renowned art school Central Saint Martins, in London, where she studied design. Her reverence for public service was key in her campaign. Her father, Colin, was an English teacher and her mother Diana worked in the NHS. Her brother, Joe, also worked in the NHS.
Edwards’s campaign, focused on tackling the cost of living crisis, boosting public services and protecting green land, helped her win the seat.
A source close to Edwards said: “She’s incredibly knowledgeable and astute. She just knows a lot about a lot.”
Upon her graduation, she co-founded Urban Brew, a design collective, before working at Oxfam on fundraising and events such as the London Marathon from 2010 to 2012. She then moved back to Moseley and began working for the Unite union. She was part of a “young leaders” programme run by the US ambassador in 2015.
She faced criticism after it was revealed that she had only recently moved to Tamworth from Moseley, which is 25 miles away.
Alistair Strathern, a former teacher turned climate consultant, became the first Labour MP to represent Mid Bedfordshire since the constituency was created in 1918. In his effort to make history, he leant on his record as a local councillor and presented himself as the antithesis of Nadine Dorries, who has been described as an “absentee MP” and had the whip withdrawn in 2012 for agreeing to appear on I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here! without being granted permission.
Strathern, 33, grew up in Bedfordshire and studied philosophy, politics and economics at St Anne’s College at the University of Oxford, where he served as the co-chairman of the university Labour club.
After graduating, Strathern worked as a maths teacher and most recently worked at the Bank of England.
In the run-up to his election, it was revealed that Strathern posed as a zombie as part of a demonstration in November 2022 to oppose the new Public Order Act outside the Home Office that was organised by Greenpeace, where his partner, Megan Corton Scott, works as a campaigner.
After the revelations, Grant Shapps, then the energy security secretary, called on Sir Keir Starmer to remove Strathern from the ballot.
• Starmer is ‘heir to Blair’: The by-elections as they happened
https://www.thetimes.com/article/starmer-is-heir-to-blair-after-wins-in-mid-bedfordshire-and-tamworth-as-it-happened-23rxszwdv
Shapps said: “One minute they are climbing the PM’s house, next they’ve got a Labour rosette on. Sir Keir Starmer must show he practises what he preaches for once, and block the eco-mob from his candidates’ list.”
Strathern described the criticism as “desperate” and while he suggested that he would continue to support Greenpeace, admitted that the action was “not the type of protest I would be attending now”.
He said: “For myself, I’ll always be someone who stands up for what I believe in, but I think it’s also important — given how our previous MP behaved — that you really respect the dignity of the office of being an MP.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Britain joins nations calling for a ban on deep sea mining
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
Britain has joined more than 20 countries backing a moratorium on deep sea mining in a significant shift given that it has previously granted licences for the practice.
The Metals Company, a Canadian firm, and Nauru, an island nation in the Pacific, are hoping to start using machines next year to extract cobalt, copper and other metals from the Pacific seabed between Hawaii and Mexico.
The company argues it would be less environmentally destructive than clearing rainforests, while conservationists fear it would open a new front and threaten thousands of unique species.
• 5,000 rare species in Pacific threatened by deep-sea mining
The UK has now come out in support of a ban on deep sea mining until the environmental impact is better understood, saying it will not sponsor or support licences. Labour has been calling for such measures for months.
Governments are meeting in Jamaica at the International Seabed Authority, the UN body responsible for mining the seabed, for talks lasting a week and a half. The members of the UN agency are yet to block deep sea mining, and the UK’s shift is no guarantee that a moratorium will be agreed.
The government said its move was part of the UK’s international advocacy on protecting the oceans, which has included the creation of huge marine parks around overseas territories.
“That is why we will use our scientific expertise to fully understand the impact of deep sea mining on precious ecosystems; and in the meantime, we will not support or sponsor any exploitation licences,” said Thérèse Coffey, the environment secretary.
The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs also said a new UK-based science network would be established to gather more data on the impact of harvesting nodules of rock that contain valuable metals used in electric vehicles and other clean technologies. The UK has previously issued licences to a subsidiary of Lockheed Martin.
Environmental campaigners welcomed the shift in stance. “Opening a new extractive industry in the absence of the necessary scientific knowledge to protect the marine environment is clearly not the right path,” said Jessica Battle, global lead for WWF’s No Deep Seabed Mining initiative. A total of 23 countries have now backed a moratorium.
Greenpeace said the government had “clawed back” some credibility as a “global ocean champion” but should support a full ban on deep sea mining.
The group also contrasted the action in seas far away with the government’s support for new licences for oil and gas drilling in the North Sea, 27 of which were awarded on Monday. Fiona Nicholls, Greenpeace UK’s oceans campaigner, said: “The climate crisis is one of the biggest threats to marine life, and more oil and gas drilling will only make it worse.”
Gerard Barron, chief executive of The Metals Company, said: “The moratorium advocated for by the UK and a minority of other member states has no legal basis under Unclos [a UN law governing use of ocean resources] or international law.”
Stanley Johnson, the former MEP, green campaigner and Boris Johnson’s father, said: “This UK stance will, I hope, strengthen the determination of those who are ready to resist current pressures to open up the seabed for unrestrained exploitation. At a time when other aspects of UK environmental policy, for example the ‘net zero reset’, are being greeted with considerable scepticism, this announcement by the UK government today is doubly welcome.”
